title: He was not searching for Jesus.
paragraphs:
He was not searching for Jesus.
He was hunting those who followed Him.

Saul of Tarsus was not neutral.
He was not curious.
He was not “on a journey.”
He was convinced… and he was wrong.

He believed he was defending God while actively fighting against Him.
He carried authority, letters, and fury—moving from city to city to silence a movement he thought was dangerous.
And then… everything changed.

Not gradually.
Not emotionally.
Not through persuasion.
But through an encounter.
On the road to Damascus, heaven interrupted a man who thought he had everything figured out.

A light brighter than the sun broke through his certainty.
A voice shattered his theology:
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” (Acts 9:4)
In that moment, Saul realized something terrifying and life-altering:
To oppose the church… was to oppose Christ Himself.
And just like that, the persecutor collapsed.

Blind.
Shaken.
Undone.
The man who walked in with authority… had to be led by the hand.
This is where most people miss the power of Paul’s story.

It’s not just that he changed.
It’s how God chose him.
Because if we’re honest… Saul is not the kind of person most people would trust with a future in ministry.

He had blood in his history.
Fear attached to his name.
Damage connected to his past.

If Saul showed up in most modern spaces, many would question him.
Some would avoid him.
Others would disqualify him completely.
But God didn’t consult public opinion.

Acts 9:15 says:
“He is a chosen instrument of Mine…”
Chosen.

Not after years of proving himself.
Not after rebuilding his reputation.
Not after earning trust back from everyone.
Chosen in the middle of his brokenness.
This is the scandal of grace.

God does not choose based on résumé.
He chooses based on purpose.
And sometimes, the very person people fear the most… becomes the one God uses the greatest.
Saul became Paul.

The same man who once destroyed churches began planting them.
The same voice that once threatened believers began preaching Christ boldly.
The same hands that once approved violence began writing letters that still transform lives today.
Let that sink in.

God didn’t just forgive Paul.
He gave him responsibility.
That is a level of grace many people struggle to understand.

Because we are comfortable with forgiveness…
But uncomfortable with restoration.

We don’t mind when God saves someone.
We hesitate when He starts using them.
But Paul’s life confronts that mindset directly.

1 Timothy 1:15–16 says:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners—of whom I am the worst… But for that very reason I was shown mercy…”

Paul didn’t hide his past.
He highlighted it.
Because his story wasn’t about how good he became.
It was about how powerful God is.
Here’s the deeper lesson:
Some people are trying to change their lives without ever encountering Jesus.

They adjust habits.
They clean up behavior.
They manage appearances.
But Paul didn’t experience behavior modification.
He experienced identity transformation.

He didn’t just start doing better things.
He became a different man.
And that only happened because he met Christ.
That matters.

Because no amount of discipline can replace surrender.
No amount of effort can replace revelation.

You can be passionate and still be wrong.
You can be active and still be misaligned.
You can be religious and still be resisting God.
Paul was all three.
Until he wasn’t.
And here’s what should challenge all of us:
Who are we writing off… that God may be preparing?

Who have we labeled as “too far gone”…
when heaven is one encounter away from rewriting their entire story?
Paul’s life reminds us that grace is not limited by our comfort.

It reaches into places we would avoid.
It chooses people we would overlook.
It restores lives we would disqualify.
And it doesn’t just save them…
It sends them.

So if you feel disqualified by your past—
remember Paul.

If you feel like you’ve gone too far—
remember Paul.

If you think God could never use you—
remember Paul.

The man who once fought the church
became one of its greatest builders.

The man who once resisted Jesus
became one of His boldest voices.

The man who once carried destruction
became a carrier of truth across nations.
That is what happens when grace interrupts a life.
Not improvement.
Transformation.
So the question is not whether God can use broken people.
Scripture already answered that.
The real question is:
Will you surrender… when He calls your name?
